title: Chemical Coordination in Plants
tagline: Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene, and the tropic responses they control.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Plants have no nervous system, yet they coordinate growth precisely — the job falls to phytohormones, small organic molecules produced in one region and active at extremely low concentrations elsewhere. This chapter covers the five major groups — auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene — with their discovery, site of production and effects, then connects them to the growth responses plants show to environmental stimuli: phototropism, geotropism, hydrotropism and chemotropism. Understanding which hormone promotes and which inhibits growth explains phenomena from apical dominance to fruit ripening and the commercial use of hormone-based weedkillers.

facts.label: Five major hormones
facts.value: Auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid (inhibitor), ethylene (gaseous)

facts.label: Auxin effect
facts.value: Cell elongation; at high concentration it controls weeds (2,4-D)

facts.label: Tropisms
facts.value: Phototropic, geotropic, hydrotropic, chemotropic — directional growth set by hormone redistribution

blocks.text: Auxins were the first plant hormones discovered, following Boysen-Jensen and Paal's experiments on the phototropic oat coleoptile and Went's isolation of the growth-promoting substance in 1928. Auxin is produced at shoot tips and developing buds, promotes cell elongation, triggers bending toward light, and at high synthetic concentrations kills broad-leaved weeds — 2,4-D is the classic selective weedkiller. Gibberellins promote stem elongation, break dormancy of seeds and buds, and induce flowering; the dwarf-plant mutant of maize that responded to them established their role. Cytokinins promote cell division (cytokinesis) and are found richly in coconut milk and young fruits, delaying ageing of leaves. Abscisic acid is the growth inhibitor: it maintains seed and bud dormancy and closes stomata during water stress. Ethylene is the gaseous hormone that triggers fruit ripening and leaf fall.

items.meaning: Naturally occurring organic substance regulating plant growth in minute quantities.
Growth-promoting hormone from shoot tips causing cell elongation and phototropic bending.
Hormone promoting stem elongation, seed germination and flowering.
Hormone promoting cell division and delaying leaf senescence.
Inhibitory hormone maintaining dormancy and closing stomata under stress.
Gaseous hormone that ripens fruit and promotes abscission.

items: Auxin: shoot tip -> elongation, apical dominance, phototropic bending; synthetic form 2,4-D kills broad-leaved weeds.
Gibberellins: promote internode elongation, break seed dormancy, induce flowering in rosette plants.
Cytokinins: promote cell division, delay senescence, encourage shoot formation in tissue culture.
Abscisic acid: growth inhibitor; dormancy, stomatal closure in drought, abscission promotion.
Ethylene: gaseous; fruit ripening and leaf/fruit fall; produced by ripening fruit itself.
Hormones act at parts distant from production — this is true chemical coordination.

items.text: Spraying gibberellin on seedless grapes increases fruit size; sprayed on sugarcane it elongates the stem.
items.note: Commercial agriculture uses hormone effects routinely — a favourite exam application.

items.text: Bananas ripen faster in a paper bag because trapped ethylene accumulates.
items.note: The fruit produces its own ripening hormone; the bag simply prevents its dispersal.

items.text: 2,4-D kills dandelions in a lawn but not the grass — synthetic auxin at concentrations toxic to broad-leaves only.
items.note: Selectivity comes from dose sensitivity differences between plant types.

blocks.text: Tropisms are directional growth responses to stimuli, and auxin redistribution is the common mechanism. In phototropism, light causes auxin to migrate to the shaded side of the shoot, where the higher concentration accelerates cell elongation — the shoot bends toward the light. In the root, the same accumulated auxin at high concentration INHIBITS elongation, so the root bends downward: this differential sensitivity explains why shoots are positively phototropic while roots ignore light. Geotropism follows gravity — auxin accumulates on the lower side; the shoot grows down (positive), the root grows down as well (positive geotropism) because auxin inhibits root elongation on the lower side, slowing it and curving the root down. Hydrotropism bends roots toward moisture regardless of gravity, and chemotropism is growth toward a chemical stimulus, as in pollen tube growth toward the ovule.

items: Phototropism: shoot bends toward light (positive); auxin accumulates on the shaded side and promotes elongation.
Geotropism: roots grow down (positive), shoots grow up (negative) — gravity detected by starch-filled statoliths in root caps.
Hydrotropism: roots grow toward higher water potential, overriding gravity when soil dries unevenly.
Chemotropism: directional growth toward a chemical, e.g. pollen tube growing down the style to the ovule.
Same hormone, opposite effect in shoot and root: elongation promoted in shoots, inhibited in roots at that concentration.
Mechanism of all tropisms: unequal distribution of auxin across the organ.

items.text: Darwin's experiment: covered the tip of a coleoptile — no bending; covered only the base — bending continued.
items.note: Shows the stimulus is perceived at the tip but the response occurs below it — a signal travels down.

items.text: A seedling on its side: root continues down, shoot curves up within hours.
items.note: Both are positively geotropic in outcome — gravity reorients growth in opposite directions for each organ.

items.text: Pollen tube grows down the style toward the ovule guided by chemical signals from the embryo sac.

items.meaning: Directional growth in response to unilateral light.
Directional growth in response to gravity; roots positive, shoots negative.
Growth of roots toward greater moisture.
Growth toward a chemical stimulus, e.g. pollen tube to ovule.
Starch grains in the root cap that settle on the lower side, detecting gravity.

blocks.text: Apical dominance is the suppression of lateral (axillary) buds by auxin produced at the shoot tip. Pinching out the tip removes the auxin source, lateral buds break and the plant becomes bushier — the principle behind pruning hedges and shaping houseplants. Fruit ripening coordinated by ethylene explains why one bruised apple spoils a whole bowl, and why commercial ripening rooms control ethylene concentration. Abscisic acid's stomatal closure under drought links hormone action directly to survival, while cytokinin application delays the yellowing of cut flowers and stored green vegetables. Every one of these applications traces to a single idea: a hormone made in one place changing growth somewhere else.

items: Pinching tips removes auxin -> lateral buds grow -> bushier plant (apical dominance released).
Ethylene controls ripening rooms; one ripe fruit accelerates others nearby.
ABA sprays could in principle close stomata and reduce wilting; the plant's own AHA does this during drought.
Cytokinins delay ageing — used to keep cut flowers and leafy vegetables fresh.
Auxin in tissue culture at specific ratios directs root versus shoot formation from callus.
Synthetic auxins (2,4-D) as selective weedkillers exploit dosage sensitivity between crops and broad-leaved weeds.

items.text: Pruning a hedge: cut tips -> no apical auxin -> axillary buds sprout -> dense growth.
items.note: The response appears days later as the lateral buds escape inhibition.

items.text: Ripening rooms expose green bananas to controlled ethylene, then hold low ethylene to slow ripening during transport.
items.note: Both promotion and suppression of the same hormone are used commercially.

figures.caption: Figure: Phototropism of a shoot tip
figures.description: Under unilateral light, auxin migrates to the shaded side; the higher auxin concentration elongates shaded-side cells, curving the shoot toward the light source.

figures.caption: Figure: Hormone effects summary
figures.description: Promoters: auxin (elongation), gibberellin (internodes, germination), cytokinin (division). Inhibitors: abscisic acid (dormancy, stomatal closure). Ripener: ethylene.

keyPoints: Phytohormones regulate growth in tiny quantities and often act at a distance from their production site.
Auxin promotes cell elongation, causes phototropic bending and enforces apical dominance.
Gibberellins promote internode elongation, break dormancy and induce flowering.
Cytokinins promote cell division and delay ageing of leaves.
Abscisic acid is the inhibitor: dormancy, stomatal closure, abscission.
Ethylene is gaseous and ripens fruit.
Tropisms: phototropic, geotropic, hydrotropic, chemotropic — all driven by unequal auxin distribution.
Auxin promotes elongation in shoots but inhibits it in roots — the same signal, opposite response.
Removing the shoot tip releases lateral buds from apical dominance.
experimentFocus: Darwin's coleoptile experiments need tip-perception versus response-below distinction — the signal, not the growth, starts at the tip.
When asked why roots grow down but shoots grow up, answer with differential auxin sensitivity, not with separate hormones.
Application questions expect the hormone, its effect, and the practical use in one chain: ethylene -> ripening -> ripening rooms.
examFocus: Name the hormone and the site of action for every effect — 'growth hormone' alone earns nothing.
Tropism answers must state which side has more auxin and whether elongation is faster or slower there.
Include both promoter and inhibitor hormones; questions often target abscisic acid precisely because students forget the inhibitor.
Pruning and weedkiller answers should name auxin explicitly, with 2,4-D for the synthetic weedkiller case.

vocabulary.meaning: Natural plant growth regulator in minute amounts.
Suppression of lateral buds by auxin from the shoot tip.
Directional growth toward or away from a stimulus.
Natural shedding of leaves or fruit.
Synthetic auxin used as a selective broad-leaved weedkiller.

questions.prompt: Which phytohormone is responsible for the ripening of fruit?
questions.explanation: Ethylene is a gaseous hormone produced by ripening fruit that accelerates ripening in surrounding fruit.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing auxin — auxin maintains growth and prevents premature ripening in many fruits.

questions.prompt: A shoot placed on its side curves upward because:
options: Auxin accumulates on the lower side and promotes elongation there
Auxin is destroyed on the upper side
Gravity kills cells on the lower side
Ethylene collects on the upper side
questions.answer: Auxin accumulates on the lower side and promotes elongation there
questions.explanation: Gravity causes auxin to settle on the lower side; in shoots the higher auxin concentration speeds elongation, curving the shoot upward (negative geotropism).
questions.commonMistake: Applying the root rule to the shoot — in roots the same accumulation INHIBITS elongation, curving downward.

questions.prompt: Pinching out the growing tip of a plant causes it to become bushy because:
options: Lateral buds are released from apical dominance
questions.answer: Lateral buds are released from apical dominance
questions.explanation: The tip is the source of the auxin that suppresses axillary buds; removing it removes the suppression, so lateral branches grow.
questions.commonMistake: Saying pinching 'stimulates' lateral buds directly — it removes an inhibitor rather than adding a stimulant.

questions.prompt: Which hormone maintains dormancy in seeds and closes stomata during drought?
questions.explanation: ABA is the growth inhibitor: it enforces dormancy and triggers stomatal closure when the plant is water-stressed.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing gibberellin, which does the opposite — it BREAKS dormancy and initiates germination.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the synthetic auxin 2,4-D is used as a ________ because it promotes uncontrolled growth in ________ plants at concentrations that spare grasses.
questions.explanation: At high concentration synthetic auxin destroys the growth control of broad-leaved weeds while the crop grasses remain unharmed.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it a hormone spray for growth — at weedkiller doses it is effectively a toxin.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the pollen tube growing down the style toward the ovule is an example of ________ tropism, while a root growing toward moisture is ________ tropism.
questions.explanation: Each tropism is named for its stimulus: chemicals for the pollen tube, water for the rooting response.
questions.commonMistake: Calling the pollen tube response geotropic — its direction follows chemical signals, not gravity.

questions.prompt: State three effects of auxin and explain how it causes a shoot to bend toward light.
questions.answer: Effects of auxin: (1) promotes cell elongation in shoots; (2) enforces apical dominance, suppressing lateral buds; (3) at high synthetic concentration it acts as a selective weedkiller (2,4-D). Bending: under unilateral light, auxin redistributes to the shaded side of the shoot. The higher auxin concentration there accelerates cell elongation relative to the lit side, so the shoot curves toward the light source.
questions.explanation: The bending explanation requires the redistribution, the unequal concentration, and the unequal elongation rate — all three steps.
questions.commonMistake: Saying light 'destroys auxin on the lit side' — modern understanding is active transport to the shaded side; either way the shaded side ends with more.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between phototropism and geotropism with an example of each.
questions.answer: Phototropism is directional growth in response to unilateral light: a sunflower shoot bends toward the light because auxin accumulates on the shaded side and elongates those cells — shoots are positively phototropic. Geotropism is directional growth in response to gravity: a root of a seedling placed on its side grows downward because gravity causes statoliths and auxin to settle on the lower side, where auxin inhibits root elongation, curving the root down — roots are positively geotropic and shoots negatively geotropic.
questions.explanation: The distinction rests on the STIMULUS (light versus gravity); examples must show the direction and the underlying hormone asymmetry.
questions.commonMistake: Giving examples without stating the stimulus — the stimulus defines the tropism name.

questions.prompt: Compare the five major phytohormones: name for each the producing region and two effects, and state which are growth promoters and which inhibitors.
questions.answer: Auxin — produced at shoot tips and young buds; promotes cell elongation and enforces apical dominance; PROMOTER. Gibberellin — produced in young leaves, roots and developing seeds; promotes internode elongation and breaks seed dormancy; PROMOTER. Cytokinin — produced in root tips and young fruits; promotes cell division and delays leaf ageing; PROMOTER. Abscisic acid — produced throughout the plant, especially in mature leaves; maintains dormancy and closes stomata under water stress; INHIBITOR. Ethylene — produced in ripening fruit and stressed tissues; ripens fruit and promotes leaf/fruit abscission; inhibitory in effect and gaseous in form.
questions.explanation: Five hormones with site, two effects and promoter/inhibitor status; grouping them by action makes the comparison memorable.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting that ethylene is gaseous and abscisic acid is the inhibitor — those two facts are the most common dropped marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why the same concentration of auxin that makes a shoot elongate would inhibit a root, and state how this difference is useful to the plant.
questions.answer: Shoot and root cells differ in their sensitivity to auxin: roots respond to very low concentrations while shoots need much higher ones for maximal elongation. A concentration that is optimal for elongating shoot cells exceeds the optimum for roots and therefore inhibits root cell elongation. The usefulness is directional growth: when gravity makes auxin accumulate on the lower side of a horizontal seedling, the root grows downward (lower side elongates more slowly, curving the root down) while the shoot grows upward (lower side elongates faster, curving it up), so both organs end up oriented correctly — roots into moist soil, shoots toward light.
questions.explanation: The dose-response difference explains the paradox, and the developmental payoff — correct orientation of both organs — completes the answer.
questions.commonMistake: Saying roots receive a 'different hormone' — it is the same auxin; only the tissue sensitivity differs.
